title: Pizza Marinara
subtitle: The oldest Neapolitan pizza: tomato, garlic, and oregano
excerpt: Pizza Marinara is the oldest recorded Neapolitan pizza: tomato, garlic, dried oregano, and olive oil, with no cheese. The sauce is intense and the garlic roasts into something sweet and mellow under the heat of a very hot oven.
sourceNotes: Pizza Marinara predates the Margherita and is listed in the EU Traditional Specialities Guaranteed register for authentic Neapolitan pizza. It takes its name from the fishermen (marinai) of Naples who kept the long-life toppings of garlic, tomato, and oregano on their boats, not from any fish topping.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Prepare the dough 24 hours ahead. Mix the sauce and slice the garlic up to 1 hour before baking.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan or conventional, maximum oven setting. Preheat with a heavy tray or pizza stone inside for at least 45 minutes.

content.text: Pizza Marinara is the simplest pizza in the Neapolitan canon: tomato, garlic, oregano, and olive oil. No cheese. The absence of mozzarella is not a shortcut but the point. Without cheese to melt over them, the garlic and oregano roast directly in the oven heat and the tomato concentrates to a deep, slightly charred sauce.
You need one 210 g ball of 24-hour pizza dough per pizza, rested at room temperature for 2 hours before shaping.
Heat the oven to its maximum setting with a heavy tray or pizza stone on the top shelf. Preheat for at least 45 minutes.
Season the passata with salt and stir. Slice the garlic as thinly as you can.
Stretch one dough ball to a rough 30 cm disc on a lightly floured surface, leaving a 2 cm border for the rim.
Spread passata over the disc. Scatter the garlic slices evenly, then sprinkle with dried oregano. Drizzle olive oil generously over the top.
Slide onto the hot tray and bake for 8 to 10 minutes until the rim is charred and the garlic slices are golden and slightly crisp at the edges. Eat immediately.

The Marinara is the oldest of the classic Neapolitan pizzas, predating the Margherita by at least a century. The name comes from the fishermen who kept these toppings on their boats because garlic, tomato, and dried oregano do not spoil quickly. It has nothing to do with seafood, and never did.
